title: UN General Assembly adopts the partition plan (Resolution 181)

altNames.name: United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine

place.name: General Assembly Hall, Flushing Meadow, New York (the New York City Pavilion, now the Queens Museum)
place.note: Far from Palestine: the UN General Assembly met in this building from 1946 to 1951, before the UN headquarters in Manhattan was finished. The building is now the Queens Museum.

summary: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly, meeting in its temporary hall at Flushing Meadow, New York, voted 33 to 13, with 10 abstentions, for a plan to divide British-ruled Palestine into independent Arab and Jewish states, with Jerusalem under international control, once the British Mandate ended. Jewish leaders accepted the plan, though with misgivings. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it, arguing that it denied the Arab majority its right to self-determination. Fighting broke out in Palestine the next day.

title: Attacks on two Jewish buses near Fajja

place.name: Near Fajja, on the road from Netanya towards Jerusalem
place.note: Fajja was an Arab village that was depopulated in 1948. Accounts place the first ambush at Fajja or nearby Kfar Sirkin; Britannica says 'near Lod (Lydda)'.

summary: On 30 November 1947, the day after the UN vote, Arab gunmen ambushed a Jewish bus travelling from Netanya to Jerusalem as it drove through the village of Fajja, killing five passengers; soon afterwards they attacked a second bus, killing two more. These were the first deaths of the civil war, and the attack is often cited as its start. Historians disagree about whether it was a response to the UN vote or revenge for an earlier killing of five Arabs by the Jewish underground group Lehi.

accounts.claim: A reaction to the UN partition vote: Jewish news reports at the time, and traditional Zionist historiography, presented the attacks as the first Arab violence against partition.

disputes.about: where the first bus was attacked

accounts.claim: As it drove through the village of Fajja, near Kfar Sirkin.

title: Haifa oil refinery and Balad al-Shaykh massacres

altNames.name: Haifa Oil Refinery massacre
altNames.usage: common name for the killings at the refinery on 30 December

place.name: Haifa oil refinery (Consolidated Refineries), Haifa Bay, and the nearby villages of Balad al-Shaykh and Hawassa
place.note: Marker at the refinery. Balad al-Shaykh (about 32.7725, 35.0428) lay a few kilometres away; it was depopulated in 1948 and its site became Tel Hanan, now part of Nesher.

summary: On 30 December 1947 members of the Jewish underground group Irgun threw two bombs from a passing car into a crowd of Arab day labourers outside the gate of the British-owned oil refinery in Haifa, killing six. Arab workers at the refinery then attacked their Jewish co-workers, killing 39 to 41 of them, before British troops and police restored order. The Jewish Agency condemned the Irgun bombing but authorised a reprisal: on the night of 31 December–1 January, Palmach units raided the nearby Arab villages of Balad al-Shaykh and Hawassa, where many refinery workers lived, blowing up houses and killing dozens of villagers, including women and children (the number is disputed).

disputes.about: number of Jewish workers killed at the refinery

accounts.claim: 39 killed (the figure given by Ilan Pappé and Benny Morris; 39 names on the memorial at the site).
41 killed (Jewish Telegraphic Agency at the time; also Zachary Lockman, 1996).

disputes.about: number of villagers killed at Balad al-Shaykh

accounts.claim: Between 60 and 70 villagers, including women and children (Zachary Lockman; Golani and Manna; Ilan Pappé).
Haganah reports gave 'about 70 killed' in one report and 21 killed (including two women and five children) with 41 injured in another (as cited by Benny Morris).
The police figure reported at the time was at least four Arabs killed and more than 30 wounded; Haganah sources said the toll was 'considerably higher'.

title: Arab Liberation Army enters Palestine

altNames.name: Arab Salvation Army / Arab Rescue Army
altNames.usage: other English translations of the Arabic name

place.name: Northern Palestine (the Galilee and the Nablus–Jenin–Tulkarm area); headquarters at Jaba'
place.note: Marker at Jaba', the village between Nablus and Jenin where Fawzi al-Qawuqji set up his headquarters; the army's units were spread over a wide area.

summary: From January 1948, battalions of the Arab Liberation Army—volunteers from Arab countries, set up by the Arab League and commanded by Fawzi al-Qawuqji—crossed into Palestine from Syria, Lebanon and Transjordan to fight on the Palestinian Arab side against partition. They based themselves in Arab villages in the Galilee and in the Nablus, Jenin and Tulkarm districts, and British forces did not stop them entering. In early March 1948 Qawuqji set up his headquarters at the village of Jaba', between Nablus and Jenin.

accounts.claim: He arrived on 4 March 1948, according to his own account, and set up headquarters at Jab'a.
He returned to Palestine and set up headquarters at Jaba on 5 March 1948 (having briefly joined a battalion near Tubas earlier).
About 6,000 volunteers had joined by mid-March 1948, though General Ismail Safwat said the number actually deployed might have been as low as 3,500.
Between 3,000 and 5,000 foreign volunteers were serving in the army in April 1948.
British reports quoted by the UN in February 1948 described bands of about 300, 700 and 950 men entering in January, and a force of 'not less than 1400' in Samaria.

title: Semiramis Hotel bombing in Katamon, Jerusalem

place.name: Semiramis Hotel, Katamon, Jerusalem
place.note: Hotel in the Katamon neighbourhood of Jerusalem. Coordinates are those Wikipedia gives for the bombing; the exact building position was not checked.

summary: On the night of 5–6 January 1948, a Haganah team blew up the Christian-owned Semiramis Hotel in Jerusalem's Katamon neighbourhood, which the Haganah suspected was an Arab headquarters. The explosion killed 24 or 26 civilians, among them seven members of the Aboussouan family, the owner's 23-year-old son and the acting Spanish consul, Manuel Allende Salazar. The British authorities condemned the attack, and David Ben-Gurion replaced the Haganah officer in charge of Jerusalem, Mishael Shaham, with David Shaltiel.

disputes.about: whether the hotel was an Arab military base

accounts.claim: Yes: a Haganah spokesman told the Associated Press it was 'an important meeting place of Arab gangs, where arms were distributed to villages in the Jerusalem area', and the Jewish Agency stood by its statement that the hotel was a centre for Arab gangs and military groups; Wikipedia adds that the white jeep of Arab commander Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni had been seen in the hotel driveway before the bombing.

No: the Palestine (Mandate) Government said reports that the hotel was a base for Arab gangs and the headquarters of the Najjada and Futuwwa youth groups were 'entirely without foundation'; the Haganah later said it had acted on inaccurate information.

According to Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre's book O Jerusalem!, the aim was 'a major blow in Arab Katamon' that 'might force the Arabs out of the quarter and change the psychological climate in the city'.
24 or 26 civilians, including at least one child.
12 bodies recovered by 7 January, with one woman found alive in the debris (early count while rescue work went on).

title: Ben Yehuda Street bombing in Jerusalem
summary: On 22 February 1948, British Army trucks packed with explosives, driven by Arab fighters and British deserters, blew up on Ben Yehuda Street in the Jewish centre of Jerusalem, destroying several buildings, including two hotels. Around 50 people were killed (sources give 49 to 58) and well over 100 were injured, almost all of them Jewish civilians. Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni's Army of the Holy War claimed responsibility, calling it revenge for an Irgun bombing in Ramla, while Jewish leaders at first blamed the British.

title: Haganah finalises Plan Dalet (Plan D)

altNames.name: Tokhnit Dalet
altNames.usage: Hebrew (dalet is the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet)

place.name: Mandatory Palestine (country-wide plan)
place.note: A plan for the whole country with no single location; the marker uses Wikipedia's coordinates for Mandatory Palestine, which sit at Jerusalem.

summary: On 10 March 1948 the Haganah, the main Jewish military force, finalised Plan Dalet ('Plan D'), its comprehensive operational plan for the period of the British withdrawal. Its stated aim was to gain control of the territory of the planned Jewish state and of Jewish settlements outside it, and to defend them against Arab forces, including the armies expected to invade. The text allowed units to occupy Arab villages and urban neighbourhoods, to destroy villages that were hard to hold, and to expel the population where villagers resisted. Haganah offensives under the plan began in early April; historians strongly disagree about what it was really meant to achieve.

accounts.claim: Mainly a defensive military plan: it aimed to secure the area allotted to the Jewish state and Jewish settlements against the coming Arab invasion, and its expulsion clauses applied only to villages that fought and resisted occupation (Yoav Gelber; David Tal; the Haganah's own view).

A master plan for conquering as much of Palestine as possible and expelling its Arab population—'a blueprint for ethnic cleansing' (Walid Khalidi; Ilan Pappé; other historians whom Gale's dictionary describes as pro-Palestinian).
Not a blanket order to expel Palestinians, but it gave field commanders formal cover to expel or destroy villages they judged hostile, and it 'prefigured' a war of conquest (Benny Morris).

title: Operation Nachshon and the battle for al-Qastal

place.name: al-Qastal (Kastel), on the Tel Aviv–Jerusalem road
place.note: The operation covered the wider road corridor. Al-Qastal was depopulated and demolished in April 1948; the site is now Castel National Park, next to Mevaseret Zion.

summary: By late March 1948, fighters led by Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni had blockaded the road from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, leaving the city's 100,000 Jews on rations. In early April the Haganah launched Operation Nachshon, its first large-scale operation, to reopen the road, and Palmach troops took the hilltop village of al-Qastal on 3 April. Al-Husayni was killed there in the early hours of 8 April; his men retook the village, but most then left for his funeral, and the Palmach recaptured it and blew up its houses on 9 April. Several supply convoys reached Jewish Jerusalem before the road was blocked again.

title: Battle of Mishmar HaEmek

summary: On 4 April 1948 the Arab Liberation Army under Fawzi al-Qawuqji attacked the kibbutz of Mishmar HaEmek, beside the road from Jenin to Haifa, shelling it with artillery. During a 24-hour truce arranged by British troops on 7 April the kibbutz evacuated its children, then refused to surrender, and the Haganah counter-attacked. By 15 April the ALA had withdrawn. Haganah forces captured the surrounding Arab villages and destroyed them; most residents fled, and those who stayed were detained or expelled.

summary: On 9 April 1948 about 120 fighters from the Jewish underground groups Irgun and Lehi attacked Deir Yassin, a Palestinian Arab village of roughly 700 people just west of Jerusalem; they met armed resistance and were helped by Haganah and Palmach units. Around 100 to 120 villagers were killed, by most modern estimates, many of them women, children and elderly people, and the surviving villagers were forced out. The Jewish Agency and the Haganah condemned the killings. News of the massacre spread fear across Palestine and is widely seen as having sped up the flight of Palestinian Arabs from their homes.

accounts.claim: 254, the figure reported at the time by the Arab Higher Committee and repeated by the Jewish Agency, a Red Cross official and The New York Times; Ilan Pappé suggests it was deliberately inflated.

About 100 to 120, from later research: for example 107 (survivor interviews by Sharif Kana'ana of Bir Zeit University, 1988), 117 (Aref al-Aref, 1956), about 100–110 (Benny Morris), 101 (Eliezer Tauber), 110–140 (Matthew Hogan).

title: Hadassah medical convoy massacre

summary: On 13 April 1948 a convoy of ten vehicles taking doctors, nurses, patients and supplies to the Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus, escorted by Haganah armoured cars, was ambushed by Arab fighters in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of Jerusalem. The attackers shouted 'For Deir Yassin', and the attack is widely described as revenge for that massacre four days earlier. British troops nearby were slow to intervene.

title: Battle of Haifa and the departure of most of its Arab residents

altNames.name: Fall of Haifa

summary: On 21–22 April 1948, as British troops pulled back from most of Haifa, the Haganah attacked the Arab neighbourhoods of this mixed port city and took them in about a day and a half, using mortars and Arabic-language radio and loudspeaker broadcasts. On 22 April the city's Arab leaders, saying they could not enforce truce terms, told a meeting at the town hall that the Arab population wished to leave. Most of Haifa's Arabs left, many of them by sea; by mid-May only about 3,000–4,000 remained of a pre-war Arab population of more than 50,000. Why they left—on their leaders' decision or out of fear of the attackers—is strongly disputed by historians.

title: Capture of Ein al-Zeitun and killing of prisoners

place.note: Palestinian village 1.5 km north of Safed, depopulated in 1948; its houses were blown up or burned and ruins remain on the site.

summary: Ein al-Zeitun, a Palestinian village of some 800–950 people just north of Safed, was attacked by the Palmach's Third Battalion in the early hours of 1 May 1948 with mortar fire and a ground assault, as a prelude to the battle for Safed. Most villagers fled or were expelled, while dozens of men were held prisoner. According to Israeli historian Benny Morris and soldiers' testimony, dozens of prisoners were then killed in a gully between the village and Safed on the orders of battalion commander Moshe Kelman. Palmach sappers blew up or burned the village on 2–3 May, a sight that frightened and demoralised Safed's Arab residents.

Between 30 and 70 unarmed prisoners killed after the capture.
Thirty-seven men taken captive were, according to Benny Morris, probably among a group of about seventy people killed in the gully.

title: Battle of Safed
summary: Safed, a hill town in Upper Galilee with about 10,000–12,000 Arab and 1,500 Jewish residents, was fought over after British troops left in mid-April 1948. As part of Operation Yiftach, Palmach forces attacked on 6 May without success, then captured the town in a second assault on the night of 9–10 May after a heavy mortar bombardment. Almost all of Safed's Arab residents fled, and the 130 or so elderly residents who stayed were later expelled or moved out.

accounts.claim: They fled despite Jewish assurances that they would not be harmed (Israel Defense Forces account; Britannica says the Arabs fled despite Jewish authorities urging them to stay).

Flight was driven by the heavy bombardment and by fear spread by Palmach actions in the area, such as the capture of nearby Ein al-Zeitun on 1 May, after which captured men were reportedly executed and the remaining villagers expelled, and Yigal Allon's 'whispering' campaign in the Hula valley; the elderly residents who stayed in Safed were later expelled.

title: Fall of Gush Etzion and the Kfar Etzion massacre

place.name: Kfar Etzion (Gush Etzion), between Jerusalem and Hebron
place.note: The kibbutz was destroyed in 1948; it was re-established in 1967 as the first Israeli settlement in the West Bank.

summary: Gush Etzion was a bloc of four Jewish kibbutzim between Jerusalem and Hebron, in the area the UN plan gave to the Arab state; besieged for months, its fighters had attacked traffic on the main road, including Arab Legion convoys. On 12 May 1948 units of Transjordan's Arab Legion with armoured cars, joined by hundreds of local Arab fighters, attacked Kfar Etzion, and on 13 May they broke through its defences. Many defenders were shot as or after they surrendered; around 127 to 129 died at Kfar Etzion and only four survived. The other three kibbutzim surrendered and their people were taken as prisoners of war to Transjordan.
parties: local Arab irregulars from the Hebron area
Haganah, Palmach and kibbutz members of Gush Etzion

accounts.claim: 127 died in the defence of Kfar Etzion, of whom about 15 were killed after surrendering (Martin Gilbert); elsewhere 'about 129'.
151 Jewish fighters (21 of them women) killed over the two days, 127 of them on 13 May, most while or after surrendering (Benny Morris).
157 for the whole battle of Gush Etzion (Levi, 1986), or 220 (Yossi Katz).
Arab Legion soldiers together with local Arab irregulars; survivors testified that Legionnaires took part (the official Israeli version).

Men from nearby Arab villages, seeking revenge for Deir Yassin and for the destruction of one of their villages, did the killing; the Legion arrived too late to stop them (the Arab Legion version). Its commander John Glubb later wrote that 'not a single Jew was massacred at Kfar Etzion'.

A Legion officer said the defenders had not formally surrendered, that some kept shooting after others gave up, and that Legionnaires tried to defend prisoners and shot some villagers who were killing them (cited by Benny Morris).

summary: On the afternoon of Friday 14 May 1948, at the Tel Aviv Museum, David Ben-Gurion read out a declaration establishing a Jewish state 'to be known as the State of Israel', taking effect when the British Mandate ended at midnight. The text appealed to the state's Arab inhabitants to keep the peace, promising them full and equal citizenship. US President Truman recognised the new state within hours, and the next morning the armies of neighbouring Arab states entered Palestine, turning the civil war into a war between states. Israelis celebrate the date as Independence Day, while Palestinians mark 15 May as Nakba Day ('the catastrophe').

summary: On 15 May 1948, as the British Mandate ended and the day after Israel declared independence, armies of neighbouring Arab states crossed into Palestine: Egypt's from the south, Transjordan's Arab Legion and Iraq's army from the east, and Syria's at the southern end of the Sea of Galilee, while Egyptian planes bombed Tel Aviv. The Arab League told the United Nations its members were intervening 'for the sole purpose of restoring peace and security and establishing law and order in Palestine'; Israeli accounts call it an invasion of the new state. Sources differ on which states took part, especially Lebanon (see disputes). Palestinians commemorate 15 May each year as Nakba Day, remembering the mass displacement of 1948.

title: Capture of Tantura and killings of villagers

place.note: Palestinian coastal village depopulated and largely destroyed in 1948; Kibbutz Nahsholim (founded June 1948) and Dor (1949) were built on its lands, by today's Dor Beach, Israel.

summary: On the night of 22–23 May 1948, the 33rd Battalion of the Haganah's Alexandroni Brigade attacked Tantura, a Palestinian fishing and farming village of about 1,500 people on the coast south of Haifa, and captured it after a battle. What happened after the surrender is disputed: survivors, Palestinian and some Israeli historians, and several Israeli veterans interviewed decades later describe men being separated from their families, shot and buried in mass graves, while other veterans and some Israeli historians deny that a massacre took place. The surviving villagers were driven out — many women and children to nearby al-Furaydis — and the village was largely destroyed.
parties: Villagers and local defenders of Tantura

disputes.about: Whether a massacre took place after the surrender

accounts.claim: Yes: survivors' testimony collected by Palestinian and Israeli researchers describes men separated from the other villagers, shot and buried in a mass grave; Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi wrote in 1961 of the 'methodical shooting' of some forty young men, and Israeli historian Ilan Pappé of executions and 'a killing spree'.

Several Alexandroni veterans interviewed for the 2022 Israeli documentary 'Tantura' described killings of villagers after the battle ended; most said it was done by a few soldiers rather than the whole battalion.

No: Alexandroni veterans denied any massacre and in 2000 sued researcher Teddy Katz for libel over his 1998 thesis; the case exposed errors in the thesis, and Katz signed a retraction that he then tried to withdraw.

Historian Benny Morris holds that prisoners were murdered and the villagers expelled, but that documents do not show a large-scale massacre, most deaths having occurred in the fighting; in a 2022 op-ed criticising the film he wrote that some Israeli historians had concluded there were 'small war crimes committed but not a massacre'.
Historian Yoav Gelber says Katz's thesis relied mostly on oral evidence, 'good for folklore but not for history', and has called the massacre allegation a 'blood libel'.
About forty young men shot and buried in a communal grave (Walid Khalidi, 1961).
Estimates range from a few dozen to more than 200.
More than 200 non-combatants, according to Katz's research as reported by Maariv in 2000; Katz later told NPR that a man who helped bury the dead gave him the figure of 270.
Fourteen attackers and more than seventy villagers were killed in the battle itself (Benny Morris).

A 2023 investigation by Forensic Architecture, commissioned by the Palestinian NGO Adalah, judged two sites under Dor Beach parking areas 'very likely' to contain mass graves of residents executed after the battle.
After reviewing 1949 aerial images, the 2022 film concluded that even if bodies were buried under the parking lot, they are probably no longer there.

place.note: Isdud was a Palestinian Arab village; the bridge site is now at the eastern entrance to Ashdod, Israel.

summary: Egypt's main column advanced up the coast and on 28 May halted at a bridge over the Lakhish River just north of the village of Isdud, about 30 km south of Tel Aviv, which Israeli forces had blown up. On 29 May the new Israeli air force made its first strike, with four just-assembled fighter planes, and on 2–3 June the Givati Brigade attacked Isdud but was driven back with heavy losses. Even so, the Egyptian army advanced no further north and switched to holding the territory it had taken. Israelis later named the bridge site Ad Halom ('thus far').

disputes.about: Did Egypt intend to drive on to Tel Aviv?

accounts.claim: Yes: the Egyptian column was aiming at Tel Aviv and was stopped here — the view in David Ben-Gurion's diary and in Israeli commemoration of the battle.

No: most historians agree Egypt was not intending to advance to Tel Aviv; Arab historians such as Mustafa Kabha and Muhammad Nimr al-Hawari describe Egypt's Tel Aviv declarations as for show, with no real plan to go beyond Isdud.

disputes.about: Was the battle a turning point?

accounts.claim: Yes: traditional Israeli historiography, the Egyptian officer Kamal Ismail ash-Sharif and Israeli historian David Tal see it as the moment Egypt was forced onto the defensive; the air strike is 'thought to have changed the course of the war'.
Not decisively: later Arab sources and some New Historians dispute this; Benny Morris sees the halt as a turning point but calls it a mistake to portray the operation as 'the crucial action'.

Iraqi reinforcements then arrived from the south and counter-attacked, and by 4 June the Israelis had been driven back. title: Battle of Nitzanim

summary: Nitzanim, a kibbutz founded in 1943 among the Arab localities of Isdud and Majdal, lay inside the area the UN partition plan gave to the Arab state and was cut off. On 7 June 1948 the Egyptian Army attacked it with artillery, aircraft, tanks and infantry, and that afternoon 105 surviving defenders, 26 of them wounded, surrendered. Thirty-three defenders were killed, and the prisoners were taken to Egypt and returned in March 1949. It was the first major Egyptian victory of the war and one of the few Israeli surrenders.

title: First truce

place.name: Palestine (whole country)
place.note: Applied across Palestine; point is Wikipedia's coordinate for Mandatory Palestine. The UN Mediator's headquarters were on Rhodes, with UN military observers in the field.

summary: On 29 May the UN Security Council called on both sides to stop fighting for four weeks, not to bring in new fighters or weapons, and to accept supervision by the UN Mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte of Sweden. After both sides accepted and terms were negotiated, the truce took effect on 11 June 1948. Both sides used the pause to reinforce and reorganise — Israel in particular imported large quantities of weapons — and Bernadotte reported three serious violations, including the Altalena arms ship. He also proposed a political settlement, which both sides rejected; the Arab states refused to extend the truce, and fighting resumed on 8 July, a day before it was due to end.
parties: United Nations (Security Council; Mediator Folke Bernadotte)

disputes.about: Whether the ban on new weapons and fighters was respected

accounts.claim: Neither side respected the truce; Israel imported large quantities of arms, mainly from Czechoslovakia (about 25,000 rifles, 5,000 machine guns and fifty million bullets by its end), its army grew from about 30,000–35,000 to almost 65,000, and both sides sent fresh units to the front.

The Mediator reported that, apart from the Altalena, the Arabs filed only two specific complaints about Jewish arms imports, that supervision in the Arab states was 'not adequate', and in July judged that 'on the whole, the truce has worked well'.
Israel accepted the Mediator's proposals to prolong the truce, the Arab states rejected them, and hostilities broke out again on 8 July.
On 8 July, the day before the truce expired, Egyptian forces under General Muhammad Naguib launched an offensive, pre-empting a planned Israeli offensive in the south.

title: Altalena affair

altNames.name: Altalena
altNames.usage: name of the Irgun arms ship

place.name: Tel Aviv beach (Frishman Street); first landing at Kfar Vitkin
place.note: The ship first landed men and arms at Kfar Vitkin beach (about 32.382, 34.877) on 20–21 June, then ran aground off Tel Aviv, where it was shelled on 22 June.

summary: The Altalena, a ship bought by the Irgun — one of the Jewish armed groups then being merged into the new Israel Defense Forces — reached the beach at Kfar Vitkin on 20 June, during the truce, carrying about 940 volunteers and a large cargo of weapons. After talks broke down over who would control the arms, David Ben-Gurion's government ordered the army to seize them; fighting broke out on the beach, and on 22 June the army shelled the ship off Tel Aviv, setting it on fire. Sixteen Irgun members and three soldiers were killed, and Irgun units in the army were then broken up. The clash is remembered in Israel as the moment the new state came close to civil war.
parties: Israel Defense Forces (Alexandroni Brigade, Palmach, navy)

accounts.claim: The government feared an Irgun coup and 'an army within an army'; Ben-Gurion told the cabinet that if Begin did not hand over the weapons, 'we will open fire', and the army was empowered to use force.
The ten-minute ultimatum was 'insulting and unrealistic'; Begin ordered his men not to shoot back and the ship raised a white flag, but automatic fire continued at survivors in the water.
Which side fired first at Kfar Vitkin is disputed; eyewitness Hillel Kook said the Irgun fired first, shooting toward the sea.
Yigal Allon later said the shells were warning shots that hit the ship by accident; journalist Shlomo Nakdimon wrote that Ben-Gurion had earlier told the air force to sink the ship at sea.
The UN Mediator treated the landing as one of three serious truce violations and described the government as taking 'strong police action to prevent the landing'.

title: Capture of Lydda and Ramle and expulsion of their inhabitants

altNames.name: Lydda death march
altNames.usage: name used for the forced march of Lydda's inhabitants

place.name: Lydda (Lod)
place.note: Renamed Lod after its capture; neighbouring Ramle (Hebrew: Ramla) lies just to the south-west (about 31.928, 34.863). Both towns were resettled with Jewish immigrants.

summary: In Operation Dani, launched as the first truce ended, Israeli forces surrounded Lydda and Ramle — two Arab towns on the Tel Aviv–Jerusalem road that the UN partition plan had assigned to the Arab state — and took Lydda on 11 July and Ramle on 12 July 1948. On 12 July, after Arab Legion armoured cars entered Lydda and a firefight broke out, Israeli troops shot at people in the streets and houses and killed detainees in the Dahmash mosque; the death toll is disputed. Over the following days some 50,000–70,000 residents and refugees left the towns, those from Ramle mostly by bus and truck and those from Lydda on foot in summer heat toward the Arab Legion's lines, and some died on the march. Most historians, drawing on Israeli army orders and Yitzhak Rabin's memoirs, describe this as an expulsion; Yigal Allon, the operation's commander, denied that any expulsion order was given.
parties: Israel Defense Forces (Yiftach, Kiryati and 8th Armoured Brigades; 89th Battalion)
Residents of Lydda and Ramle and refugees sheltering there

disputes.about: Number killed in Lydda on 12 July

accounts.claim: Some 250 Palestinians killed between 11:30 and 14:00, citing the Palmach's own history (Benny Morris).
426 killed in Lydda on 12 July, 176 of them in the mosque (Palestinian historian Aref al-Aref); 250–400 killed (Nur Masalha).
Dozens, perhaps as many as 200, killed between 9 and 13 July, with 80–176 killed inside the Dahmash mosque (citing Salman Abu Sitta's Atlas of Palestine).
Israeli historians Alon Kadish and Avraham Sela: no direct first-hand evidence of a massacre; the deaths occurred in a battle for the town. This view has been widely criticised.

disputes.about: Deaths on the march from Lydda

accounts.claim: 'A handful and perhaps dozens' died of dehydration and exhaustion (Benny Morris).
About 500 died, 350 of them from thirst and exhaustion (Aref al-Aref); 335 (Nimr al-Khatib, a figure Morris calls an exaggeration); 350 (Nur Masalha).
Old men, women and children fell by the wayside, dying of exhaustion, dehydration and disease.

Expelled on army orders: an order signed by Yitzhak Rabin on 12 July said the inhabitants of Lydda 'must be expelled quickly'; Rabin later wrote that 'the population of Lod did not leave willingly', a passage removed by Israeli censors from his memoirs and published by the New York Times in 1979.

No expulsion order: Yigal Allon said in 1979 that neither he nor Ben-Gurion gave one, and that residents left because the Arab Legion ordered the town cleared for a counter-attack and because of panic.

The UN Mediator's report of September 1948 said Israeli forces occupied Ramleh, Lydda and other places 'most of whose inhabitants fled', and that many late-comers among the refugees were 'deprived of everything'.
Historian Yoav Gelber attributes the expulsions to Allon rather than to a Ben-Gurion order.

title: Surrender of Nazareth

summary: In Operation Dekel, Israeli forces advanced through Lower Galilee against the Arab Liberation Army and local fighters, capturing many villages. Nazareth — a largely Christian Arab town that the UN plan had assigned to the Arab state, already crowded with refugees — surrendered on 16 July after little resistance, under a written agreement promising that its civilians would not be harmed. When brigade commander Ben Dunkelman was ordered to expel the town's Arab residents he refused, and David Ben-Gurion backed him, fearing an outcry in the Christian world. Unlike Lydda and Ramle, most of Nazareth's people stayed, and the town became a refuge for Arabs displaced from the surrounding area.

summary: In July 1948 Irgun and Lehi units, by then coordinated by the new Israel Defense Forces but still independent, planned with the IDF's Etzioni Brigade to break into Jerusalem's walled Old City and capture East Jerusalem. Set for the evening of 16 July, a day before the second truce, the attack was repeatedly delayed and began only at 02:30. The Irgun broke through at the New Gate, but the Lehi attack on the wall towards the Jaffa Gate and the Beit Horon Battalion's attack from Mount Zion failed, and at 05:45 commander David Shaltiel ordered a retreat. The Old City stayed in Jordanian hands until the 1967 war.

summary: On 15 July the UN Security Council declared the situation in Palestine a threat to the peace and ordered all sides to stop fighting — in Jerusalem within 24 hours and everywhere else within three days — warning of further action if they did not. The cease-fire took effect first in Jerusalem and then, on 18 July, in the rest of the country, ending the 'Ten Days' of fighting. Unlike the first truce, it had no fixed end date. In those ten days Israeli forces had extended the territory they held, taking Lydda, Ramle and Nazareth, while the Arab Legion kept Latrun.

title: Operation Shoter: capture of Ijzim, Ein Ghazal and Jaba'

summary: Ijzim, Ein Ghazal and Jaba', three Palestinian villages south of Haifa known as the 'Little Triangle', had beaten off Israeli attacks on 18 June and 8 July 1948, and their fighters blocked traffic on the Tel Aviv–Haifa coastal road. After the second truce began on 18 July, Israel presented its attack as a 'police operation' against residents of territory it considered its own; the villages were bombed from the air and then attacked by Alexandroni, Golani and Carmeli brigade units on 24–25 July. They fell on 26 July, the road was reopened, and almost all of the villagers, about 7,000–8,000 people, fled or were driven out, many to the Jenin area. A UN investigation later found the attack unjustified and a breach of the truce, but Israel refused its demand to let the villagers return.

title: Assassination of UN mediator Folke Bernadotte

place.name: Katamon quarter, Jerusalem

summary: On 17 September 1948 Count Folke Bernadotte, the Swedish diplomat serving as the UN's mediator in Palestine, was shot dead in Jerusalem together with a French UN observer, Colonel André Sérot. The gunmen belonged to Lehi (the 'Stern Gang'), a Jewish underground group that opposed his new peace proposals, presented the day before, which would have given the Negev to the Arab side and Galilee to Israel and called for Arab refugees to be allowed to return home. The UN Security Council condemned the killing and Israel's government outlawed Lehi, but the police investigation never identified the killers. His American deputy, Ralph Bunche, took over as acting mediator.

accounts.claim: The UN report on the killing said the Provisional Government of Israel 'must assume the full responsibility' for the assassinations and had done little to curb a press campaign against the mediator; the Security Council asked Israel to report on its investigation but received no report.
The Swedish government believed Bernadotte had been killed by Israeli government agents and publicly attacked the inadequacy of the Israeli investigation.

In the Israeli official view the killers were the 'Stern Gang', which Israel's foreign minister had told the UN existed in Israel only as a political organization; after the killing the government outlawed Lehi and arrested many of its members. Wikipedia adds that the government had already decided to reject Bernadotte's plan.

title: All-Palestine Government formed in Gaza

place.name: Gaza
place.note: City-level location. Gaza was then held by the Egyptian army; the government later moved to Cairo.

summary: Backed by Egypt, the Arab League announced on 20 September 1948 that an Arab government for the whole of Palestine would be formed with its seat in Egyptian-held Gaza; it was established there on 22 September, with Ahmad Hilmi Abd al-Baqi as prime minister. On 1 October a Palestinian National Council meeting in Gaza under Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti of Jerusalem, declared the independence of the whole of Palestine. The government had no real administration, money or army of its own and depended on Egypt, while King Abdullah of Transjordan opposed it. After Egypt's defeats later in 1948 it moved to Cairo.

disputes.about: how independent the government really was

accounts.claim: Historian Avi Shlaim calls it 'an Egyptian-led phantom deliberately created by the Arab states' to answer public opposition to partition and to challenge Transjordan's claim to Arab Palestine, while granting that in its first three weeks it was a genuine Palestinian attempt to assert independence.

Some regard it as the first attempt to establish an independent Palestinian state; many questioned its credentials as a sovereign government because it relied on Egyptian military, political and economic power.

summary: When Operation Yoav cut the Egyptian army's lines in October 1948, about 4,000 Egyptian soldiers were encircled around the Arab villages of al-Faluja and Iraq al-Manshiyya, east of Gaza. They held out under siege for about four months; among them was an officer, Gamal Abdel Nasser, later Egypt's president. Under the Egypt–Israel armistice of 24 February 1949 the Egyptian troops withdrew to Egypt on 26 February and the area passed to Israeli control, with written guarantees for the safety of the roughly 3,140 Arab civilians there. By late April 1949 those civilians had left; how they came to leave is disputed (see disputes).

title: Operation Yoav and the capture of Beersheba

summary: On 15 October 1948 Israel launched Operation Yoav against the Egyptian army in the northern Negev, ending the second truce on this front. Israeli forces broke through the Egyptian lines, opened a land route to the Jewish settlements in the Negev, and on 21 October captured the town of Beersheba from its Egyptian garrison after several hours of fighting. A UN-ordered truce took effect on 22 October, leaving an Egyptian brigade encircled around al-Faluja. Most of Beersheba's Arab residents had fled during Israeli air raids, and the roughly 350 who were still there were expelled to Gaza.

accounts.claim: Israeli accounts: Egypt had broken the truce by blocking Israeli convoys to the Negev, and the offensive followed an Egyptian attack on an Israeli supply convoy (dated 15 October in the IDF account published by the Jewish Virtual Library; 14 October in Wikipedia and in Israel's letter to the UN Security Council of 8 November 1948).

UN Acting Mediator Ralph Bunche said the Israeli action was on a scale that 'could only be undertaken after considerable preparation, and could scarcely be explained as simple retaliatory action'; Wikipedia notes that the operation had been approved at an Israeli cabinet session on 6 October.

title: Operation Hiram in the upper Galilee

altNames.name: Mivtza Hiram
altNames.usage: Hebrew operation name, after Hiram, the biblical king of Tyre

place.name: Upper Galilee
place.note: Regional marker. The fighting covered the upper Galilee held by the Arab Liberation Army, and Israeli forces crossed into southern Lebanon as far as the Litani River.

summary: After the Arab Liberation Army (ALA) seized an Israeli hilltop position near kibbutz Manara on 22 October 1948, four Israeli brigades attacked the ALA and a Syrian battalion in the upper Galilee on the night of 28–29 October. In about 60 hours, before a ceasefire on 31 October, Israel took the whole upper Galilee, an area the 1947 UN partition plan had assigned to the Arab state, and pushed into southern Lebanon as far as the Litani River. Tens of thousands of Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled to Lebanon, and killings of villagers and prisoners were reported in several places, including Safsaf, Eilabun and Hula in Lebanon.
parties: Arab villagers of the upper Galilee

Launched on 24 October 1948.

disputes.about: flight or expulsion of the Arab population

accounts.claim: More than 50,000 Palestinians were 'expelled from their homes'; on 31 October the front commander, Moshe Carmel, ordered that 'the inhabitants of the areas conquered should be assisted to leave'.

An estimated 50,000 fled into Lebanon, some ahead of the advancing forces and some expelled from villages that had resisted, while people in villages that had stayed at peace were allowed to remain and became Israeli citizens.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (via the Jewish Virtual Library): in Galilee the Israeli advance 'was followed by only a minor exodus of the Arab population'; many Muslims left, but most Christians and almost all Druze stayed.

Massacres were reported at Safsaf (50–70 men killed, according to Israeli records and survivors), at Eilabun (14 men killed, 12 of them executed after the village surrendered, according to Wikipedia; villagers interviewed by Al Jazeera also spoke of 14 young men killed and the expulsion of the rest on foot) and at Hula in Lebanon (35–58 captured men shot). Historian Benny Morris writes that the main official Israeli response was flat or qualified denial.

Israel's UN representative answered Arab League charges of atrocities in Upper Galilee on 8 November 1948 by saying that none of the League's 'atrocity stories' had on investigation 'proved to have had the least substance or foundation'.

summary: During Operation Yoav, on 29 October 1948, the Israeli army's 89th Battalion (8th Brigade) captured al-Dawayima, a large Arab village west of Hebron that was crowded with refugees, meeting little or no resistance. Soldiers then killed many of the people who remained, including women and children, and the rest of the population fled. An Israeli army intelligence inquiry at the time put the dead at about 100, while Israel's representative at the UN told the Security Council that the village had been abandoned before Israeli forces took it. How many were killed is disputed.

summary: Safsaf, a village near Safad defended by the Arab Liberation Army's Second Yarmuk Battalion, was the first village taken in Operation Hiram; it fell to the Israeli army's 7th Brigade on 29 October 1948 after a battle. Israeli records from the time and survivors' accounts both describe soldiers tying up and shooting dozens of the village's men after the capture, and raping several women. The remaining villagers left for Lebanon in the following days. The Israeli army opened internal inquiries, but their reports remain classified.

title: UN General Assembly Resolution 194

summary: Meeting in Paris on 11 December 1948, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 194 by 35 votes to 15, with 8 abstentions. It set up a Conciliation Commission of three states (France, Turkey and the United States) to carry on the work of the murdered mediator Bernadotte, called for the Jerusalem area to be placed under UN control, and resolved that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so, with compensation for those choosing not to return. The six Arab League states then in the UN voted against it, and Israel, not yet a UN member, objected to many of its articles.

accounts.claim: A UN study says the resolution's importance lies in 'its specific establishment of the right of peaceful return of the Palestinians to their homes', a right the General Assembly has reaffirmed every year.

A pro-Israel fact sheet argues that the UN 'resolved that only those refugees willing to live at peace should be repatriated and that others should be compensated and resettled', and that the Arab states rejected the resolution at the time and reinterpreted it only after losing the war.
Wikipedia notes that it has been argued the resolution enshrines a right of return for Palestinian refugees, 'a claim that Israel disputes'.

summary: On 22 December 1948 Israel launched Operation Horev to drive the remaining Egyptian forces out of the Negev. title: Operation Uvda reaches Umm Rashrash

summary: On 5 March 1949, while armistice talks with Transjordan were under way, Israeli brigades set out from Beersheba and other bases to take control of the southern Negev down to the Red Sea, an area the 1947 UN partition plan had allotted to the Jewish state. They met no significant resistance, as Jordan's Arab Legion pulled back, and on 10 March they reached the abandoned police post of Umm Rashrash on the Gulf of Aqaba, where soldiers raised a hand-drawn 'Ink Flag'. It is often counted as the last military operation of the war, and the Israeli town of Eilat was founded on the site in 1949.

disputes.about: whether the advance broke the truce

accounts.claim: UN Acting Mediator Ralph Bunche reported on 22 March 1949 that since 8 March Israeli forces in more than normal patrol strength had moved into the area between the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba and taken up positions they had not held before, and that any positions set up there by either side since the truce of 18 July 1948 were contrary to its terms; he also found that small Arab patrols had violated the truce.

Wikipedia says that while negotiating with Jordan, and despite Bunche's insistence that the ceasefire be strictly observed, Israel carried out operations to occupy large parts of the central and southern Negev.

Israel told the UN on 10 March that its forces were nowhere operating outside Israel's borders and had not crossed the Transjordan frontier; Israeli accounts describe the operation as establishing sovereignty over territory allotted to the Jewish state, rather than conquering it.

title: Lausanne Conference

place.name: Lausanne, Switzerland
place.note: City-level location; the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine held its meetings with the delegations in Lausanne.

summary: From 27 April 1949 the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine (France, Turkey and the United States) held talks in Lausanne, Switzerland, with delegations from Israel and from Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. Because the Arab delegations refused to meet the Israelis directly, the Commission talked with each side separately. On 12 May both sides signed protocols accepting a working document, with the 1947 partition map attached, as a basis for discussion, but they stayed far apart on refugees and borders. The Commission suspended its Lausanne meetings in mid-September 1949 without an agreement.

accounts.claim: Israel argued the protocol was merely a 'procedural device' and that signing it did not mean accepting the 1947 partition borders. At the signing its delegate, Walter Eytan, said his delegation fully reserved its position, which the Commission chairman took to mean Israel could reject parts of the partition boundaries and propose others while using the plan as a point from which to work; Eytan confirmed that this was his meaning.

Arab leaders argued that the protocol did mean acceptance of the partition borders; a UN study says it reiterated the international commitment to a Palestinian Arab state on the basis of the partition resolution, subject to Israeli reservations.

Israel: refugees could be dealt with only within a general peace settlement linked to territory, and the solution should be sought primarily in resettling refugees in Arab territories.

summary: On 11 May 1949 the UN General Assembly, meeting in plenary at Flushing Meadow, New York, voted 37 to 12, with 9 abstentions, to admit Israel as a member state, meeting the two-thirds majority required; Assembly President H. V. Evatt then formally declared Israel admitted. The vote, Resolution 273, followed a Security Council recommendation (Resolution 69 of 4 March 1949) and a debate in the Assembly's Ad Hoc Political Committee at Lake Success. There, Israel's representative Abba Eban was asked how Israel would carry out the Assembly's earlier resolutions on Jerusalem (181) and on the refugees (194), and said Israel would cooperate on the refugee resolution. Arab states voted against, and the United Kingdom was among the countries that abstained.
